why: Ascending order in a BST is its in-order traversal. The iterator is that traversal paused between steps: keep a stack of the left spine still to visit, pop for next, then push the left spine of the popped node's right child.
hints: The values must come out in ascending order. Which traversal of a BST produces that?
Do the in-order traversal lazily: a stack holds the nodes whose left side is done but which have not been returned yet. The top of the stack is always the next smallest value.
Init: push the root and all its left descendants. next: pop, push the left spine of its right child, return the value. hasNext: the stack is nonempty. Amortised O(1) per call, O(h) memory.
pitfalls: Return every result as a string: values as decimal text, hasNext as "true"/"false".
Do not flatten the whole tree up front if you want the intended O(h) memory (it still passes, but misses the point).
hasNext must not advance the iterator.
statement:
You are given the root of a binary search tree with unique values, and a list of operations, each either "next" or "hasNext". Simulate one iterator that visits the values in ascending order:

  • "next" returns the next smallest value not yet returned (it is always valid).
  • "hasNext" returns whether any value remains, without moving the iterator.

Return the results as strings, in operation order: numbers as decimal text, booleans as "true" or "false".

Example. root = [7,3,15,null,null,9,20] holds 3, 7, 9, 15, 20 in ascending order. Operations ["next","next","hasNext","next","hasNext"]:

  1. next gives "3".
  2. next gives "7".
  3. hasNext: 9, 15 and 20 remain, so "true".
  4. next gives "9".
  5. hasNext: 15 and 20 remain, so "true".

Answer: ["3","7","true","9","true"].
